The So-iuy mullet (Planiliza haematocheilus) attains a maximum reported total body length of 80 centimeters [Li = 80 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger members of the Mugilidae family in the northwestern Pacific. Field surveys conducted in the Sea of Japan and the Yellow Sea indicate that this species reaches such dimensions only after several years of sustained growth, with the largest individuals typically captured in offshore winter aggregations. Females ultimately reach a maximum wet body mass of 3837 grams [Wwi = 3837 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the largest specimens encountered in commercial catches. This substantial adult mass reflects the considerable energetic investment required for the seasonal spawning migrations that characterise the reproductive biology of this coastal mugilid. The onset of sexual maturity, however, occurs well before such maximal dimensions are achieved. Puberty is reached when individuals attain a total length of approximately 48 centimeters [Lp = approximately 48 centimeters], at which point the corresponding wet body mass averages about 850 grams [Wwp = about 850 grams], marking the transition from the juvenile phase to reproductive competence.

At the other extreme of the life history spectrum, the initial biological mass of a newly formed individual is remarkably small. The eggs of Planiliza haematocheilus, which are demersal and adhesive, measure approximately 0.7 millimeters in diameter, and the resulting freshly fertilised ovum yields a wet weight of just 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This minuscule starting mass underscores the extreme fecundity that characterises this species, as females must compensate for the high mortality rates endured by the tiny, lecithotrophic yolk-sac larvae that emerge following eclosion. The chorion rupture releases a prolarva that depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days after hatching, before the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition to active feeding on planktonic prey begins. The shift from endogenous to exogenous nutrition represents a critical bottleneck in the early life cycle, and the capacity for rapid growth during this period is contingent upon favourable thermal conditions and adequate food availability in coastal nursery habitats.

The maximum reproductive output of the So-iuy mullet has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. Laboratory experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C] have demonstrated that individual females produce approximately 6484 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 6484 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season, a remarkably high daily fecundity that reflects the species' strategy of batch spawning over an extended reproductive window. Given that gravid females may remain reproductively active for several months under these optimal thermal conditions, the total annual egg production per female can reach prodigious numbers. This daily rate of oviposition, achieved only at the height of reproductive activity and under the warmest portion of the species' thermal range, represents an extreme allocation of somatic resources toward gamete production. The energetic cost of sustaining such high fecundity is substantial, and field-collected gravid individuals often show reduced body condition indices compared to non-reproductive conspecifics, suggesting a trade-off between current reproductive effort and somatic maintenance.

The lifespan of Planiliza haematocheilus is closely tied to thermal regime, with the longest documented survivorship recorded under the same warm-water conditions that promote rapid reproductive output. In captivity, under a constant temperature of 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C], individuals have been maintained for up to 6 years [am = up to 6 years], though wild populations likely experience higher mortality rates due to predation, fishing pressure, and the physiological demands of repeated spawning migrations. This longevity of approximately six years is comparable to that reported for other temperate mugilids, though the fast growth rate and early maturation at 48 centimeters [Lp = 48 centimeters] total length suggest a life history strategy that prioritises early reproductive output over extended somatic growth. The species is iteroparous, with females returning to spawn in successive years after reaching maturity, and the accumulation of reproductive experience may enhance spawning success in older, larger individuals approaching the ultimate length of 80 centimeters [Li = 80 centimeters].

Comparative analyses among mugilid species reveal that the So-iuy mullet occupies an intermediate position along the fast-slow life history continuum. While the maximum adult female mass of 3837 grams [Wwi = 3837 grams] is modest relative to that of the giant mullet Mugil cephalus, which can exceed 5000 grams, the reproductive output of Planiliza haematocheilus is unusually high for a fish of its size. The wet weight at puberty of 850 grams [Wwp = 850 grams] corresponds to roughly 22 percent of the ultimate female mass, a proportion that aligns closely with the typical mugilid pattern of maturation at approximately one-quarter of asymptotic size. The egg mass of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] is consistent with the production of small, pelagic-type offspring that depend on high fecundity for population persistence. Future studies investigating the metabolic costs associated with the high daily spawning rate observed at 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C] would help clarify the energetic constraints that ultimately limit the lifespan to 6 years [am = 6 years] in this commercially valuable coastal species.
